analysis.one_liner: Bans racial profiling by all law enforcement and ties federal police grants to anti-profiling policies.
analysis.headline: The End Racial and Religious Profiling Act, backed by 29 senators, never got a vote or even a hearing in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died there.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make racial profiling illegal for every police agency in the country — federal, state, local, and tribal. It would let the Justice Department or an individual sue over profiling, require federal agencies to adopt anti-profiling policies, and require states and cities to keep those policies in place to keep receiving federal police grants. It would also force the collection and publication of data on who gets stopped and searched.
analysis.who_benefits: People who face being stopped, searched, or investigated because of their race, ethnicity, national origin, religion, gender, gender identity, or sexual orientation — disproportionately Black, Latino, Muslim, and immigrant communities. Everyone who lives in those communities, since the bill funds anti-profiling training and complaint systems for their local police.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits racial profiling by every federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement agency and agent, defined as relying on actual or perceived race, ethnicity, national origin, religion, gender, gender identity, or sexual orientation in stops, searches, or investigations.

Lets the Justice Department or an individual who was profiled sue for relief in state or federal court, with disparate impact counting as prima facie evidence and attorney's fees recoverable from government bodies.

Conditions federal police grants (Byrne JAG and COPS programs) on states and cities maintaining anti-profiling policies, training, data collection, and a complaint procedure or independent audit, with the Attorney General required to withhold funds from agencies that do not comply.

Requires federal law enforcement agencies to maintain anti-profiling policies, and directs the Attorney General to issue national regulations for collecting stop-and-search data by race, ethnicity, national origin, gender, and religion, with annual public reports to Congress.

analysis.who_pays: Police departments, which would face new training, data collection, complaint handling, and possible lawsuits or withheld federal grant money if they keep profiling practices. Taxpayers would fund the grants and the data program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Law enforcement agencies and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The costs are real for police agencies: departments would need to build data systems, retrain officers, and establish complaint procedures and audits, and small or rural departments with thin budgets would bear the same paperwork burden, which is why the bill reserves them an equitable grant share.

The ban is broad: it covers reliance 'to any degree' on any listed characteristic, with a narrow exception only for trustworthy locality-specific information linking a person to an identified incident, and critics could argue it restricts the range of factors officers may use and invites litigation through the disparate-impact provision.
Enforcement through grant withholding risks cutting off police funding to the very communities the bill is meant to protect if agencies choose to lose the money rather than change practices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is a nationwide, legally enforceable prohibition on profiling plus public data on who gets stopped and searched, paid for mostly through grant conditions and a modest data program (about $5.5 million authorized for the demonstration project). The honest cost is administrative: departments would need systems, training, and audits, and the profiled communities themselves would depend on agencies choosing compliance over forfeiting grants. The design includes mitigations — funding reserved for small and rural agencies, data privacy limits, and a savings clause preserving existing civil rights remedies — but none of this got to be tested, because the bill never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee two days after introduction, and the committee never acted on it before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Ben Cardin introduced the bill on February 16, 2017, with 27 Democratic and 1 Independent cosponsor already attached, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
That referral to Judiciary was the only committee action; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded in the action history, which ends with the referral.
Congress adjourned on January 3, 2019 without the Senate taking any further action, so the bill died in committee and would have needed to be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies that would have faced new oversight, mandatory data collection, and profiling lawsuits are better off, because the bill never advanced past a committee referral.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies that avoided profiling oversight

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (federal, state, local, tribal)
industries.note: The bill would directly regulate police departments: mandatory anti-profiling policies, officer training, stop-and-search data collection, complaint procedures or independent audits, possible grant withholding, and individual profiling lawsuits with attorney's fees. Police departments do not profit from this bill but bear all its obligations, which is why it is their interest against the public's here.

The bill authorizes grants to buy technology for accurate data collection and feedback systems that flag officers at risk of profiling misconduct, creating a modest market for compliance tools that would also help communities see how their police behave.

industries.industry: Civil rights legal advocates and litigators
industries.note: The bill opens a new federal cause of action with attorney's fees available to prevailing plaintiffs, creating work for civil rights lawyers whose interest in representing profiled individuals runs alongside the public's.

industries.industry: Independent police auditors and training providers
industries.note: Grants are designated for anti-profiling training programs, independent audit programs, and administrative complaint procedures, funding auditors and trainers whose accountability role serves the same communities the bill targets.
